area: Area III. Airport and Seaplane Base Operations
objective: By the end of this lesson you can enter, fly and leave the traffic pattern at towered and non-towered airports to commercial standards, holding pattern altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots, and you can explain which pattern rules are regulations and which are recommendations.
why: A significant number of midair collisions and near midair collisions happen in airport traffic patterns, towered and non-towered [[16:14|AC 90-48E 16.1]]. As a commercial pilot you will fly faster airplanes, carry people who trust you, and share patterns with jets, so a predictable, stabilized pattern is part of the job.

prereading.what: Non-towered airport practices: traffic flow, CTAF calls, straight-ins, practice approaches, wake, entry, departure and right-of-way.
prereading.label: AC 90-66C paras 8.2 to 11.10

prereading.what: Pattern components, the key to pattern operations, upwind-side entries, and pattern altitudes for piston and turbine airplanes.
prereading.label: AC 90-66C Appendix A

prereading.what: Towered airports, leg names, pattern altitudes, right traffic, visual indicators, unexpected maneuvers and runway selection.
prereading.label: AIM 4-3-1 to 4-3-6

prereading.what: The regulations: turn direction, tower radio contact, Class D altitudes, departures and clearances.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.126 to 91.129

prereading.what: Why eyes miss traffic, reaction time, scanning, blind spots, night scanning and technology limits.
prereading.label: AC 90-48E paras 8 to 16

prereading.what: Wake vortex strength, behavior near the ground, avoidance procedures and pilot responsibility.
prereading.label: AIM 7-4-1 to 7-4-9

prereading.what: Wrong-surface landings and the stabilized approach concept, with go-around criteria.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 9, 9-4 to 9-6

warmup: Which of these must you do by regulation, and which are only recommended: enter on a 45° to downwind, make left turns at a non-towered airport, fly the pattern at 1,000 feet AGL, and talk to the tower before 4 NM at a towered airport in Class E airspace?

key_terms.def: The altitude flown in the pattern. Recommended: 1,000 feet AGL for propeller airplanes and at least 1,500 feet AGL for large and turbine-powered aircraft, unless the Chart Supplement publishes another [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3a]].
The path straight ahead along the extended centerline after takeoff, continuing at least 1/2 mile past the runway end and to within 300 feet of pattern altitude [[33:238|AIM 4-3-2c1]].
In the current AIM, the straight-ahead extension of the departure leg that ATC uses for separation, spacing or sequencing [[33:238|AIM 4-3-2c2]].
Landing without entering the pattern. The FAA discourages it under VFR, and it gives no priority over pattern traffic [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g4]].
Broadcasting your call sign, position, altitude and intentions on the CTAF, mainly at airports without an operating tower or FSS [[17:7|AC 90-66C 9.8]].
A constant-angle glide path to a chosen point on the runway, at a constant final descent airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
Low Level Wind Shear Alert System. It detects wind shear around the airport edge; controllers give the airport wind and then the boundary wind [[33:249|AIM 4-3-7a]].
A small, intense downdraft that spreads out in all directions at the surface, making both vertical and horizontal wind shear [[34:107|AIM 7-1-24a]].
Two counter-rotating vortices trailing behind every aircraft in flight, a by-product of lift [[34:147|AIM 7-4-1]].
An aircraft on a collision course seems motionless for a long time, then suddenly fills the windshield [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.8]].

chunks.title: Towered, non-towered, and the rules that apply

body.p: At the commercial level, know which pattern items are regulations (must) and which are recommendations (should). The FAA regulates the traffic pattern flow, meaning the direction of turns, not how you enter the pattern [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1]].

head: Rule
What it requires
rows: 91.126 (Class G)

Approaching to land without an operating tower: powered fixed-wing aircraft turn left unless approved light signals or visual markings show right turns [[60:451|14 CFR 91.126(b)]]. At an airport with an operating tower: two-way radio before 4 NM, up to and including 2,500 feet AGL [[60:452|14 CFR 91.126(d)]]
91.127 (Class E)
Comply with 91.126 and any part 93 patterns. The same tower radio rule: before 4 NM, up to and including 2,500 feet AGL [[60:452|14 CFR 91.127]]
91.129 (Class D)

Two-way radio before entering and while inside [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(c)(1)]]. Circle to the left unless ATC says otherwise [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(f)]]. A clearance to take off, land, or use a runway or taxiway [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(i)]]. Also comply with 91.126 and 91.127 [[60:452|14 CFR 91.129(a)]]
No more than 200 knots IAS at or below 2,500 feet AGL within 4 NM of the primary airport of a Class C or D area, unless ATC authorizes or requires otherwise [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(b)]]

callout.text: VFR radio failure in Class D: you may land if the weather is at or above basic VFR minimums, you keep visual contact with the tower, and you receive a clearance to land [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)(2)]]. A steady green light means cleared to land [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

body.p: Not every towered airport has Class D airspace. Without weather reporting, the controlled airspace normally starts at 700 or 1,200 feet AGL, but you still talk to the tower [[33:237|AIM 4-3-2a]]. That is why 91.126(d) and 91.127(c) carry a tower radio rule.

Towered: make the first call about 15 miles out [[33:237|AIM 4-3-2a]]. The tower may have you enter at any point or fly straight in. Jets and heavy airplanes often fly wider and higher patterns [[24:165|AFH 8-1]].

Non-towered: nobody is watching for you, so you take over that job. Monitor the CTAF and broadcast your intentions at least 10 minutes before taxi and at least 10 miles out when arriving [[17:6|AC 90-66C 9.5]].

callout.text: A part-time tower that is closed leaves a non-towered airport. The 91.126 traffic flow rules still apply in Class E and Class D airspace, which matters most when a towered airport is operating as a non-towered one [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1.1]].

check.q: You are inbound to an airport with an operating tower that sits in a Class E surface area. When must you first talk to the tower?
check.a: Before 4 NM from the airport, up to and including 2,500 feet AGL [[60:452|14 CFR 91.127(c)]].

head: Aircraft
Recommended pattern altitude
rows: Propeller-driven
Large and turbine-powered
Not less than 1,500 feet AGL, or 500 feet above the established pattern altitude [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3a]]
Helicopters
500 feet AGL, closer to the runway, sometimes on the opposite side [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3a]]
Any aircraft
A TPA published in the Chart Supplement replaces these, and cloud clearance (91.155) may require a different altitude [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3a]]

callout.text: In Class D the 1,500-foot figure becomes a regulation for large or turbine-powered airplanes: enter the pattern at least 1,500 feet above the airport and hold it until lower is needed for a safe landing. On departure they climb to 1,500 feet above the surface as rapidly as practicable [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(e)(1)]] [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(g)(2)]].

body.p: Speed: at most towered airports, pattern traffic typically flies no faster than 200 knots, and it is sensible to do the same at non-towered airports. Adjust your speed to fit the other traffic [[24:165|AFH 8-1]]. Fly the POH/AFM landing procedures [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.9]]. Typical piston singles fly 70 to 90 knots on downwind [[24:169|AFH 8-5]].
Size: you may vary the size of the pattern to suit your airplane's performance [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3b]]. Downwind is normally about 1/2 to 1 mile from the runway [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].

callout.text: One altitude for everyone. A common pattern altitude is the key factor in cutting collision risk at airports without an operating tower [[17:23|AC 90-66C App A]].

body.p: The checkride standard: hold pattern altitude ±100 feet and the appropriate airspeed ±10 knots (ACS CA.III.B.S5).

check.q: The airport is 1,450 feet MSL and publishes no pattern altitude. You are flying a turboprop single. What is the lowest recommended pattern altitude, in MSL?
check.a: 2,950 feet MSL. Turbine-powered aircraft enter at not less than 1,500 feet AGL [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3a]], and 1,450 + 1,500 = 2,950.

body.p: Arrive at pattern altitude and give yourself time to see the whole pattern before you join. Entering while descending creates collision hazards [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.3]].

head: Point
What you do there [[33:241|AIM FIG 4-3-2]]
rows: Enter in level flight, abeam the midpoint of the runway, at pattern altitude
Hold pattern altitude until abeam the approach end of the landing runway
Complete the turn to final at least 1/4 mile from the runway
Continue straight ahead until beyond the departure end
Staying in the pattern: turn crosswind beyond the departure end, within 300 feet of pattern altitude
Leaving: straight out, or a 45° turn in the pattern direction, beyond the departure end after reaching pattern altitude

body.p: From the downwind side: fly a 45° entry aimed at a point abeam the runway midpoint [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.3]]. Make the entry leg long enough to see the entire pattern and plan your path [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].

From the upwind side (preferred method): announce, then cross midfield at least 500 feet above pattern altitude, normally 1,500 feet AGL. If large or turbine aircraft use the airport, stay at 2,000 feet AGL. About 2 miles clear, scan, descend to pattern altitude, and turn to enter on the 45° at midfield. The alternate is a midfield crosswind entry at pattern altitude, but not when the pattern is busy [[24:168|AFH 8-4]] [[17:19|AC 90-66C App A]].

callout.text: The FAA discourages VFR straight-in approaches. If you fly one anyway, self-announce about 8 to 10 miles out and coordinate. A straight-in pilot, IFR or VFR, has no priority over aircraft in the pattern [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g4]].

body.p: Practice instrument approaches at non-towered airports (common for instrument-rated commercial students): announce when departing the FAF inbound, when established on the final segment, when the approach is completed or terminated, and when starting the missed approach [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g6]]. Give direction and distance from the airport plus your intentions, such as "6 miles south inbound VOR approach Runway 36, landing full stop," because a non-instrument pilot may not know where your fixes are [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.11.5]]. Coordinating with pattern traffic, it may be safest to break off the approach and enter downwind [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.4.2]]. If the airport has right traffic, circle to the right [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.3]].

At a tower, follow the controller's entry. Suggested headings or entry directions given to VFR pilots are advisory aids, not radar vectors, and you remain responsible for seeing and avoiding other aircraft [[33:239|AIM 4-3-2d]].

check.q: You arrive from the side opposite downwind at a non-towered field where business jets operate. Using the preferred entry, how high do you cross midfield?
check.a: 2,000 feet AGL, so you stay clear of the jets' higher pattern, then descend about 2 miles clear and join on the 45° [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

chunks.title: Departing and staying in the pattern

bullets: Takeoff or go-around: continue straight ahead until beyond the departure end of the runway, watching for pattern traffic [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.6]].

Staying in the pattern: turn crosswind beyond the departure end and within 300 feet below pattern altitude, then turn downwind at pattern altitude. The crosswind leg may be longer or shorter on unusually hot or cold days [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.7]].

Leaving: go straight out, or turn 45° (left for left traffic, right for right traffic) beyond the departure end after reaching pattern altitude. Check for traffic entering first [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.8]].
The departure leg runs at least 1/2 mile beyond the departure end and up to within 300 feet of pattern altitude [[33:238|AIM 4-3-2c1]].

body.p: Before takeoff at a non-towered airport, announce your runway, your direction of flight, or that you will stay in the pattern [[17:6|AC 90-66C 9.5.3]]. Don't enter the runway until you have checked for landing traffic aligned with your runway or landing toward you [[17:6|AC 90-66C 9.5.1]].

callout.text: An IFR release, or ATC saying "released," is not a takeoff clearance. Announce on the CTAF and make sure no one is on short final first. Don't accept an immediate departure just to meet a void time [[17:14|AC 90-66C 10.4.4]].
Lights, Camera, Action before taking the runway: lights on, transponder on, then read back (tower) or announce make, registration and model (CTAF) [[16:10|AC 90-48E 10.4.1]].

body.p: On a go-around, once at a safe altitude, make a shallow-bank turn to the upwind side of the airport. This gives you a better view of the runway and departing aircraft [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

check.q: Pattern altitude is 1,000 feet AGL and you are staying in the pattern. What is the lowest height to start the crosswind turn, and where?
check.a: 700 feet AGL (within 300 feet below pattern altitude), and only after you are beyond the departure end [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.7]].

chunks.title: Choosing the runway, pattern and weather information

body.p: Take off and land on the runway most nearly aligned into the wind. If you use a secondary runway, for example for length, stay out of the flow to the main runway [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.5]]. If others are already in the pattern, use their runway [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11]].

At a tower, ATC assigns the runway most nearly into the wind when the wind is 5 knots or more, or the calm-wind runway below 5 knots, unless another runway is operationally better or a runway use program is in effect. If you need a different runway, ask [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6b]].

head: Source
What it gives you
rows: ATIS
Recorded weather, runway and approach in use at busy airports. Updated with each official weather report. Give the letter code on first contact [[33:212|AIM 4-1-13a]] [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13]]
ASOS/AWOS
One-minute weather within about 25 NM, below 10,000 feet. At an uncontrolled field you have more current weather than a distant controller [[33:274|AIM 4-3-27]]
UNICOM
Wind and recommended runway on request. Not required to answer, no standards for what is said [[17:5|AC 90-66C 9.3]]
LLWAS, TDWR, ITWS, WSP
Wind shear and microburst information that controllers relay. The Chart Supplement lists which airports have them [[33:249|AIM 4-3-7]] [[33:250|AIM 4-3-7e]]
Sectional and Chart Supplement
Right traffic as "RP" plus runways; "*RP" means special conditions, see the Chart Supplement [[33:240|AIM 4-3-3d]]

callout.text: Wind in ATIS, ASOS and AWOS voice broadcasts is magnetic [[34:89|AIM 7-1-10]], and so is wind from the tower and the runway numbers [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6a]]. No conversion needed.

body.p: No information by radio? Check the wind and landing direction indicators from above pattern altitude, then fly well clear before descending to enter [[17:14|AC 90-66C 11.2]]. The large end of a wind sock points into the wind. The small end of a tetrahedron points toward landing, but use extreme caution with it in light or calm wind [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4b]]. Mentally enlarge the traffic pattern indicator for your runway and the base and final legs appear [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4c]].

Left traffic is the standard. Airports set right traffic where obstacles, terrain or noise-sensitive areas require it [[17:14|AC 90-66C 11.1]]. Right patterns are not shown on charts for airports with full-time towers [[33:240|AIM 4-3-3d]].

check.q: The tower reports wind 040 at 3. The airport has Runways 4-22 and 13-31, and 31 is the calm-wind runway. Which runway should you expect?
check.a: Runway 31. With wind below 5 knots, ATC normally uses the calm-wind runway [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6b]].

body.p: The examiner expects quick, sure answers about what you see on and around the runway (ACS CA.III.B.S1).

head: Item
What it tells you
rows: Runway number
Magnetic azimuth to the nearest 10°. Parallel runways add letters, left to right as seen on approach [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6a]]
Displaced threshold
White arrows lead to a 10-foot white bar. The area behind it is for takeoffs either way and landings from the opposite direction only [[33:141|AIM 2-3-3]]
Yellow crosses at each end
Runway temporarily closed. Some closures have no markings, so check NOTAMs and ATIS [[33:161|AIM 2-3-6e]]
Runway holding position marking
Four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed; hold on the solid side. Non-towered: cross only with adequate separation from others [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a]]
Mandatory sign
White inscription on red: a runway or critical area entrance, or no entry [[33:162|AIM 2-3-8]]
Taxiway location sign
Yellow on black with a yellow border: the taxiway you are on [[33:165|AIM 2-3-9]]
Rotating beacon
White and green: lighted land airport. In a Class B, C, D or E surface area, a daytime beacon often means visibility under 3 miles or ceiling under 1,000 feet [[33:133|AIM 2-1-9]]
Runway edge and end lights
Edge lights white; on instrument runways yellow on the last 2,000 feet or half the runway, whichever is less. End lights red toward the runway, green outward [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4]]
REIL
Two synchronized flashing lights beside the threshold for fast runway-end ID [[33:126|AIM 2-1-3]]
Pilot-controlled lighting
Key the mic 7 times in 5 seconds for highest, 5 for medium or lower, 3 for lowest. Start with 7 [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]]

body.p: PAPI: a row of lights, normally on the left side. Two white and two red is on the glide path (3°). Three white is slightly high, all white is high; three red is slightly low, all red is low. It gives obstacle clearance within 10° of the centerline out to 3.4 NM. Don't start down on it until you are lined up with the runway [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2b]].

callout.text: In Class D, an airplane landing on a runway with a visual approach slope indicator must stay at or above its glide path until a lower altitude is needed for a safe landing [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(e)(3)]].

check.q: On final, the PAPI shows one white and three red. What does that mean, and what do you do?
check.a: Slightly low, about 2.8° [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2b]]. Add power and raise the pitch attitude together to shallow the descent until you see two white and two red [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

body.p: The right-of-way rules apply all through the pattern. When a rule gives another aircraft the right-of-way, give way and don't pass over, under or ahead of it unless well clear [[17:11|AC 90-66C 9.12.4]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].

head: Situation
Who has the right-of-way
rows: Distress
The aircraft in distress, over all other traffic [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(c)]]. The FAA treats an airplane landing itself under emergency autoland as in distress [[16:14|AC 90-48E 14.1]]
Converging, same category
The aircraft to the other's right [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]]
Different categories

Balloon over all; glider over powered aircraft; aircraft towing or refueling over other powered aircraft; airship over other powered aircraft except one towing or refueling [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]]
Overtaking
The aircraft being overtaken. The overtaking pilot alters course to the right and passes well clear [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(f)]]
Final approach or landing
Over aircraft in flight or on the surface, but may not force off an aircraft that has landed and is clearing the runway [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]
Two aircraft approaching to land
The lower one, but it may not cut in front of or overtake one on final [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]

body.p: Gliders, including the tow plane while towing, have the right-of-way over powered aircraft [[17:16|AC 90-66C 12.2.1]]. Ultralight vehicles must yield to all aircraft [[17:17|AC 90-66C 12.3.1]].

Spacing at a tower: controllers sequence you from what they see and what pilots report. They expect minor maneuvering such as shallow S-turns, but not a 360. Never make a 360 in the pattern without first advising the controller, unless asked to or in an emergency [[33:244|AIM 4-3-5]] [[33:245|AIM 4-3-5]]. If told to report a "2-mile left base," join the extended centerline for a 2-mile final [[16:11|AC 90-48E 11.1.4]].

Spacing at a non-towered airport: adjust course or speed to fit in before you join downwind [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]. Don't announce your sequence ("number 3 to land"); that is ATC's job at towered airports [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.1]]. Avoid the words "to" and "for," which can be confused with runway numbers or altitudes [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.3]].

callout.text: Accepting traffic information, an instruction to follow an aircraft, or a visual approach means you accept responsibility for safe intervals and wake turbulence separation [[34:153|AIM 7-4-8b]].

check.q: You are on a 1-mile final. A faster airplane, lower than you, calls a short base for the same runway. Who has the right-of-way?
check.a: You do. The lower aircraft may not use its altitude to cut in front of an aircraft on final approach [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]. Still watch it and be ready to go around.

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: a commercial-standard pattern

body.p: Here is a non-towered arrival in a complex single. Speeds, power and flap settings come from your POH/AFM [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.9]].

bullets: 1. Well before the airport: get the ASOS/AWOS, set the CTAF, and brief pattern altitude, direction and runway. Do the checklists early so you can look outside [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].
2. About 10 miles out: self-announce your position, altitude and intentions, and listen for others [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.1]].
3. Descend to pattern altitude well clear of the pattern, then enter level on the 45° at midfield [[17:14|AC 90-66C 11.2]] [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.3]].
4. Downwind, 1/2 to 1 mile out: do the before-landing checks and extend the landing gear [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]. Hold pattern altitude ±100 feet and your speed ±10 knots (ACS CA.III.B.S5).
5. Abeam the approach end: reduce power and start down [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]. Extend flaps in steps on downwind, base and final so pitch and power changes stay small [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

6. About 45° past the approach end: medium-bank turn to base [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.4]] [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]. Target about 1.4 VSO, crab to keep the track square, and check final for traffic before turning [[24:173|AFH 9-2]] [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].
7. Final: finish the turn at least 1/4 mile out [[33:241|AIM FIG 4-3-2]]. Verify the runway number and alignment [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. Fly the POH speed, or 1.3 VSO if none [[24:174|AFH 9-3]].

body.p: Stabilized approach criteria for a typical piston airplane [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]:

head: Item
Stabilized when
rows: Glide path
Constant, typically 3°, to the touchdown zone
Heading
Tracking the centerline with only small corrections; bank normally 15° or less on final
Airspeed
Within +10/-5 knots of the recommended landing speed; with a gust factor added, never below the recommended speed
Configuration
Landing configuration, gear extended, in trim
Descent rate
Generally 500 to 1,000 fpm; if more than 500 fpm, reduce it before 300 feet AGL
Power
Appropriate for the configuration, not below the AFM minimum for approach
Briefings and checklists
Done before the approach, except the landing checklist

callout.text: Go around if you are not stabilized by 500 feet above the airport in VMC (1,000 feet in IMC). In a typical GA pattern, go around at once if the approach becomes unstabilized below 300 feet AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

body.p: Read the runway picture: on a stabilized approach the runway keeps the same shape as it grows. If the approach gets shallow, the runway looks shorter and wider; if it gets steep, longer and narrower [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].
Gusty air: many pilots add half the gust factor to the normal approach speed, within the AFM/POH [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

check.q: Your POH landing speed is 75 KIAS. Passing 400 feet AGL on a VFR final you see 88 KIAS. Are you stabilized, and what do you do?
check.a: No. The window is 70 to 85 KIAS (+10/-5), and you are below 500 feet in VMC, so go around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

body.p: The pattern is a rectangular course around the runway. Angle into the wind on each leg so the ground track stays square [[24:152|AFH 7-6]].

head: Turn (landing into the wind)
Bank and amount of turn [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]
rows: Downwind to base
Tailwind, high groundspeed: start with a relatively steep bank and turn more than 90°, angling toward the runway side
Base to final
Medium bank; less than 90°, because you were already angled into the wind
Departure to crosswind
Shallow bank; less than 90°, holding an angle into the wind
Crosswind to downwind
Medium bank; more than 90°, with groundspeed rising as you turn

body.p: The rule: higher groundspeed needs a steeper bank, lower groundspeed a shallower one [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]. With a tailwind on downwind, don't descend too much before base [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]. With a strong wind on final, put the base leg closer to the runway [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

Orientation: know where the runway is at every moment. At night, fly toward the beacon until you can see the runway lights, identify the threshold and edge lights before entering, and set the heading bug to runway heading as a reference for the legs. Distance and height are deceptive at night, so cross-check the altimeter and airspeed [[24:227|AFH 11-10]].
Parallel runways: don't overshoot final or fly a track that crosses the final approach or departure path of the parallel runway [[33:243|AIM FIG 4-3-3]].

callout.text: Overshooting final? Don't steepen the turn to fix it. If you are rushing the turn, go around [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

check.q: Landing Runway 27 in left traffic with wind 300 at 15. On base you fly about north toward the centerline. Which way do you crab, and why?
check.a: Crab left, into the wind from the west. Otherwise you drift east, farther from the runway, and your track is no longer perpendicular to the centerline [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

body.p: Failure to see and avoid is the most probable cause of midair collisions [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]. Most reported ones in the pattern happen on final and short final [[24:171|AFH 8-7]]. They usually happen in daylight and good visibility, between aircraft going the same direction, at or near uncontrolled airports below 1,000 feet [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].
Why eyes miss traffic, and what to do:

head: Limit
Countermeasure
rows: Refocusing from the panel to a distant aircraft takes 1 to 2 seconds [[16:5|AC 90-48E 8.1.4]]
Set up early so your eyes stay outside
The eye focuses on only about 10 to 15° at a time [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.7]]
Scan in steps of 10° or less, at least 1 second each [[16:12|AC 90-48E 12]]
Blossom effect: a collision-course target seems motionless, then fills the window [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.8]]
Keep the windshield clean; a bug smear can hide a converging plane [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.8]]
Windshield posts hide objects from one eye [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.6]]
Move your head, not just your eyes
Glare and haze [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.9]]
Keep the windshield clean; expect trouble flying into the sun [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.10]]
Night blind spot 5 to 10° wide [[16:13|AC 90-48E 13.1]]
Look about 10° off center and scan around the light

body.p: Reaction time: about 12.5 seconds pass from seeing an object until your airplane begins to move away [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]]. At a 240-knot closing speed, that is 240 × 12.5 ÷ 3,600 = about 0.83 NM of closure before you even start to turn.

Blind spots: high wings block the view above, low wings below; the worst case is a low-wing airplane above a high-wing airplane. In a climb, lower the nose briefly to see ahead; in level flight or descent, make gentle banks left and right; look behind now and then [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].

Be seen: under Operation Lights On, turn on landing lights for takeoff and below 10,000 feet, especially within 10 miles of an airport [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24c]]. ADS-B and traffic systems help, but they don't relieve you of see-and-avoid, and fixating on displays pulls your eyes inside [[16:14|AC 90-48E 15]]. Controllers have limits too, so don't depend only on their traffic advisories [[16:14|AC 90-48E 16]].

callout.text: Some aircraft have no radio, so a quiet CTAF does not mean an empty pattern [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.2]]. Also listen for "flight check" aircraft, which may fly nonstandard or opposite-direction patterns and low approaches [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.1]].

check.q: You fly a low-wing airplane on downwind. A high-wing airplane might be just below you, joining on the 45°. Who can't see whom, and what helps?
check.a: Neither may see the other: your wing blocks the view below and its wing blocks the view above. Bank gently from time to time to uncover the blind spot [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].

chunks.title: Risk: distractions, task priorities and lost awareness

body.p: Congestion, aircraft climbing and descending, and pilot preoccupation with cockpit duties all raise accident risk near the airport, more so in marginal VFR [[33:237|AIM 4-3-1]].

Situational awareness means knowing your position, your flight path, the other aircraft, the environment and the human factors in play [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. Listening to the CTAF or tower builds your mental picture of the traffic [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

bullets: Plan ahead: set frequencies, listen to ATIS/ASOS/AWOS, and finish checklists before you get busy [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].
Know the signs of overload: working harder but getting less done, then fixating on one item [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].
When overloaded: stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].
Buy time: once airborne, budget time, prioritize tasks or slow down. If rushed, ask ATC for a delay [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. On a 45° entry you can turn away, fly clear and try again [[24:169|AFH 8-5]].

body.p: AC 90-48E advises against doing checklists or chatting with passengers while taxiing, because it takes your eyes off the outside [[16:8|AC 90-48E 10.1.2]]. Bring the same discipline to the pattern, where traffic is converging on the same runway.

Disorientation: a wrong-surface landing (wrong runway, taxiway or airport) usually follows unfamiliarity, complacency or fatigue. Study the airport diagram and lighting ahead, verify the runway number on final, and go around if in doubt [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. At airports with several runways, scan for operations on the other runways [[17:11|AC 90-66C 9.12.5]].

callout.text: Avionics can lower workload or raise it. Displays can draw your attention inside the cockpit and away from the outside [[16:14|AC 90-48E 15]]. Set them up before the pattern, then fly by looking out.

check.q: What is the first sign of work overload, and what is the fix?
check.a: You work harder but accomplish less, and may fixate on one thing. Stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

chunks.title: Risk: wind shear and wake turbulence

body.p: Microbursts are small, intense downdrafts that spread out in all directions at the surface. They are hard to detect with radar or alert systems, and they can come from harmless-looking cells with little or no rain reaching the ground [[34:107|AIM 7-1-24a]] [[34:107|AIM 7-1-24b]].

head: Microburst fact
Typical value [[34:108|AIM 7-1-24]]
rows: Downdraft width
Less than 1 mile; outflow near the ground up to about 2 1/2 miles across
Strength
Downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm; surface winds up to 45 knots, a 90-knot headwind-to-tailwind shear
Life
Winds keep increasing for about 5 minutes after it hits the ground; seldom lasts more than 15 minutes
Clues
Heavy rain, light rain or virga, or just a ring of blowing dust
Company
Once they start, expect more than one in the area

body.p: The trap: the first headwind makes you balloon. If you cut power and lower the nose, you are nose-low and power-low when the tailwind hits, and you can stall or land short [[28:265|AWH 22-10]]. In an asymmetrical microburst the speed gain may be small or missing before a big loss. Be ready to go around at the first sign; at low altitude, recovery may be impossible [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].

Alerts: LLWAS gives the airport wind and then the boundary wind, for example "Wind shear alert, airport wind 230 at 8, south boundary wind 170 at 20." Basic LLWAS does not give microburst alerts [[33:249|AIM 4-3-7a]]. Systems integrated with TDWR do, for example "Runway 17 arrival microburst alert, 40 knot loss 3 mile final" [[33:250|AIM 4-3-7b]].

Wake turbulence: strength grows with weight and lower speed, so the strongest vortices come from an aircraft that is heavy, clean and slow [[34:147|AIM 7-4-3a]]. Airplanes with a short wingspan compared with the generating aircraft have the hardest time countering the roll [[34:148|AIM 7-4-3b]].
Vortices begin at rotation and end at touchdown. They sink several hundred feet per minute, and within 100 to 200 feet of the ground they drift sideways at 2 or 3 knots [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4a]].

A light crosswind of 1 to 5 knots can hold the upwind vortex in the touchdown zone, and a tailwind can move vortices forward into it. The light quartering tailwind requires maximum caution [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4b]].

head: Behind a larger aircraft
Do this [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
rows: Landing, same runway
Stay at or above its final approach path; land beyond its touchdown point
Landing, parallel runway closer than 2,500 feet
Consider drift to your runway; stay at or above its path
Landing, crossing runway
Cross above its flight path
Landing behind it departing
Land well before its rotation point
Departing behind it
Rotate before its rotation point, climb above its path until you turn clear
After its low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go
Wait at least 2 minutes before your takeoff or landing

callout.text: Visual approach behind a jet: fly on or above the glidepath. With no glidepath guidance, use 3 to 1: 3,000 feet at 10 miles, 1,500 feet at 5 miles. Aim at least 1,000 feet down the runway, above and ahead of the jet, and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:153|AIM 7-4-8e]] [[34:154|AIM 7-4-8e]].

check.q: You are cleared to land on a runway that parallels, 2,000 feet away, the runway a heavy jet is landing on. What is the concern and the plan?
check.a: The jet's vortices can drift to your runway. Stay at or above its final approach path and note its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b2]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Descending into the pattern
Be level at pattern altitude before entering; one aircraft can descend onto another [[17:19|AC 90-66C App A]]
Entry leg too short to see the traffic
Fly an entry long enough to view the whole pattern [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]
Flying too fast for the traffic
Match the other traffic's speed; typically no faster than 200 knots [[24:165|AFH 8-1]]
Big altitude or speed swings while configuring
Extend flaps in steps and retrim after each change [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]
Not assessing the wind; no wind correction
Check the wind before entering and correct on every leg [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]
Overshooting final, then steepening the turn
Go around instead [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]
Pressing on with an unstabilized approach
Use the 500-foot VMC and 300-foot pattern go-around gates [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Stretching the glide with pitch alone
Add power and pitch together; pitch alone leads to a high sink rate or a low-altitude stall [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]
Raising flaps to fix an undershoot
Don't; it can cause a sudden loss of lift and excessive sink [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
A 360 for spacing without telling the tower
Use S-turns or ask; advise the controller before any 360 [[33:245|AIM 4-3-5]]
Lining up on the wrong surface
Verify the runway number and alignment on every final [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]

check.q: You are low and undershooting on final. Why is raising the flaps a bad fix?
check.a: It may cause a sudden decrease in lift and an excessive sink rate, making things worse. Add power and pitch to level off and intercept the glide path instead [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

f1.caption: FIG 4-3-2. Traffic Pattern Operations, Single Runway.
f1.alt: Line diagram of a left-hand pattern around a single runway with numbered circles: 1 on the 45-degree entry joining downwind, 2 on downwind abeam the approach end, 3 where base turns onto final, 4 past the departure end, 5 at the turn to crosswind, and two 6s showing a 45-degree departure turn and a straight-out departure. A segmented circle with wind cone, landing direction indicator and traffic pattern indicators is drawn beside the runway, plus dashed arrows showing how to apply the traffic pattern indicators.

f2.caption: Figure 8-1. Traffic Patterns.
f2.alt: Two color illustrations of the same runway with a wind sock. The top shows a left-hand pattern in red with the entry, downwind, base, final, departure and crosswind legs, wind blowing from the far end. The bottom shows a right-hand pattern with the same legs on the other side of the runway.

f3.caption: FIG 7-4-3. Wake Ends/Wake Begins.
f3.alt: A landing airplane leaves a trail of vortex loops that ends at its touchdown point (Wake Ends). A departing airplane starts its trail of vortices at the rotation point (Wake Begins).

f4.caption: FIG 7-4-6. Vortex Movement Near Ground, with Cross Winds.
f4.alt: Front view of a jet with two vortices sinking toward the ground. With a 3-knot crosswind, the downwind vortex moves away at 6 knots (3 plus 3) while the upwind vortex stays nearly in place (3 minus 3 equals 0).

f5.caption: Figure 9-7. Change in runway shape if approach becomes narrow or steep.
f5.alt: Three cockpit views of Runway 25. Too high: the runway looks long and narrow. Proper descent angle: a normal trapezoid. Too low: the runway looks short and wide.

f6.caption: FIG 2-1-5. Precision Approach Path Indicator (PAPI).
f6.alt: Five rows of four lights: all white is high (more than 3.5 degrees); three white one red is slightly high (3.2 degrees); two white two red is on glide path (3 degrees); one white three red is slightly low (2.8 degrees); all red is low (less than 2.5 degrees).

scenario.title: Storms, a regional jet and a Class D pattern
scenario.setup: You are flying a client's retractable-gear single back to its home base, a Class D airport at 600 feet MSL with Runways 17-35 and 8-26. The ATIS gives wind 190 at 9 and thunderstorms 10 miles west moving east. Twelve miles north, the tower says: "Enter right downwind Runway 17, number two following a regional jet on a 5-mile final, caution wake turbulence." On downwind you hear: "Wind shear alert, airport wind 190 at 9, west boundary wind 250 at 25." Your passenger is filming the storm and keeps asking you questions.

questions.q: When did you need two-way radio contact, and how fast may you fly near the airport?
questions.a: Before entering the Class D airspace, and keep it while inside [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(c)(1)]]. At or below 2,500 feet AGL within 4 NM of the airport, no more than 200 knots IAS unless ATC says otherwise [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(b)]].

questions.q: Who is responsible for wake turbulence avoidance behind the jet, and how do you plan your approach?
questions.a: You are. Accepting an instruction to follow an aircraft accepts responsibility for wake separation, warning or not [[34:153|AIM 7-4-8b]] [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6a]]. Stay at or above the jet's final approach path, note its touchdown point and land beyond it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b1]].

questions.q: You are closing on the jet too fast. What may you do to fix the spacing?
questions.a: Slow down or fly shallow S-turns, which the controller expects. Don't make a 360 without first advising the controller [[33:244|AIM 4-3-5]] [[33:245|AIM 4-3-5]]. If spacing can't be fixed, go around and tell the tower [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

questions.q: What does the wind shear alert tell you, and what does it not tell you?
questions.a: It is an LLWAS report: the airport wind followed by the wind at the west edge, showing a big change in direction and speed near the airport. Basic LLWAS does not detect microbursts or shear beyond the airport edge [[33:249|AIM 4-3-7a]]. With storms nearby, think microburst: they seldom last more than 15 minutes, so holding clear or diverting is a sound choice [[34:108|AIM 7-1-24d]].

questions.q: How do you handle the passenger?
questions.a: Preoccupation and congestion near the airport raise accident risk [[33:237|AIM 4-3-1]]. Fly first: stop, think, slow down and prioritize, and ask the passenger to hold questions until you are on the ground [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

questions.q: On a 1-mile final the airspeed jumps 15 knots and you balloon above the glide path. What now?
questions.a: Treat it as the start of a microburst. Don't pull power and lower the nose, which leaves you nose-low and power-low when the tailwind hits [[28:265|AWH 22-10]]. Go around at the first sign [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].

skills.do: Identify and interpret the runway in use, markings (numbers, displaced thresholds, closed-runway crosses, hold lines), signs, the segmented circle and airport lighting, including PAPI/VASI and pilot-controlled lighting.
skills.practice: Before each flight, study the airport diagram and Chart Supplement, and on every approach say the runway, threshold type and lighting out loud. Quiz yourself on the PAPI and edge-light colors [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2b]] [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4]].

skills.do: Enter, fly and depart the pattern at towered and non-towered airports using the recommended procedures and radio calls, including upwind-side entries and departures.
skills.practice: Chair-fly each entry type with full radio calls, then fly them at several airports with your CFI. Use the AIM key to traffic pattern operations as a checklist [[33:241|AIM FIG 4-3-2]] [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.3]].

skills.do: Correct for wind drift on every leg so the ground track stays square to the runway.
skills.practice: Fly rectangular courses and pattern work on windy days. Before each turn, predict the bank and the amount of turn needed [[24:152|AFH 7-6]] [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

skills.do: Stay oriented to the runway in use, day and night, without losing sight of it.
skills.practice: Say each leg and its heading before you turn. At night, set the heading bug to runway heading [[24:227|AFH 11-10]].

skills.do: Hold traffic pattern altitude ±100 feet and the appropriate airspeed ±10 knots (ACS CA.III.B.S5).
skills.practice: Learn the downwind, descent and approach power settings for your airplane. Configure in steps and retrim after each change [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

skills.do: Keep situational awareness and proper spacing from other aircraft; extend, adjust speed or go around when needed.
skills.practice: Practice at busy airports. Build a picture of the traffic from the radio, then confirm it by spotting each aircraft before you turn [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]] [[24:169|AFH 8-5]].

quiz.q: Which of these is a regulation, not just a recommendation, at a non-towered airport in Class G airspace?
options: Entering on a 45° to downwind
Making all turns to the left unless markings or light signals show right turns
Self-announcing 10 miles out
Flying the pattern at 1,000 feet AGL
quiz.why: Turn direction is in 14 CFR 91.126(b) [[60:451|14 CFR 91.126(b)]]. The FAA regulates pattern flow, not entry; entry methods, calls and altitudes are recommended practices [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1]].

quiz.q: Unless ATC authorizes otherwise, what is the maximum indicated airspeed at or below 2,500 feet AGL within 4 NM of the primary airport of Class D airspace?
options: 156 knots
180 knots
200 knots
250 knots
quiz.why: 200 knots IAS [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(b)]]. The 250-knot limit is for flight below 10,000 feet MSL in general.

quiz.q: You depart Runway 22, which has right traffic, and want to leave the pattern with a turn. What is recommended?
options: A 45° right turn beyond the departure end, after reaching pattern altitude
A 45° left turn beyond the departure end, after reaching pattern altitude
A right turn at 500 feet AGL over the runway
A climbing turn onto downwind, then depart from midfield
quiz.why: Go straight out or exit with a 45° turn in the pattern direction (right for a right pattern) beyond the departure end after reaching pattern altitude [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.8]].

quiz.q: If you choose a VFR straight-in approach at a non-towered airport, what is the guidance?
options: Announce at 3 miles; you have priority once on final
No announcement is needed if you have a transponder
Announce once on short final so you don't block the frequency
Announce about 8 to 10 miles out and coordinate; you have no priority over pattern traffic
quiz.why: Self-announce about 8 to 10 miles out and coordinate. Straight-in pilots, IFR or VFR, have no priority over aircraft in the pattern [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g4]].

quiz.q: At a towered airport, the wind is 030 at 3 knots. What runway will ATC normally assign?
options: The runway most nearly into the wind
The longest runway
The calm-wind runway
Whatever runway the pilot requests
quiz.why: ATC assigns the runway most nearly into the wind when the wind is 5 knots or more, or the calm-wind runway below 5 knots, with some exceptions [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6b]].

quiz.q: For a typical piston airplane, what airspeed range counts as stabilized on final?
options: ±5 knots of the recommended landing speed
+10/-5 knots of the recommended landing speed
±10 knots of the recommended landing speed
+15/-0 knots of the recommended landing speed
quiz.why: Within +10/-5 KIAS of the recommended landing speed. If you add a gust factor, don't let the speed decay below the recommended speed [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

options: Glare that blooms across a dirty windshield
Night lights that seem to grow when you stare at them
A wake vortex expanding as it sinks
Two aircraft on a collision course seem motionless, then one suddenly fills the window
quiz.why: On a collision course the other aircraft seems stationary and doesn't grow for a long time, then suddenly blooms into view [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.8]].

quiz.q: You are taking off behind a larger airplane that just departed. Where should you lift off?
options: Before its rotation point, then climb above its path
After its rotation point, then stay below its path
At its rotation point, then match its climb
Anywhere, because a departing airplane's wake rises
quiz.why: Rotate before the larger aircraft's rotation point and climb above its climb path until you turn clear of its wake [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b6]].

quiz.q: The tower says "Wind shear alert, airport wind 160 at 6, north boundary wind 240 at 22." What system is this, and what can't it do?
options: TDWR; it can't measure surface wind
LLWAS; basic LLWAS gives no microburst alerts
ASOS; it can't detect wind shear
ITWS; it can't report boundary winds
quiz.why: LLWAS gives the airport wind followed by the boundary wind. It detects shear around the airport edge but does not provide microburst alerts [[33:249|AIM 4-3-7a]].

takeaways: Turn direction and tower radio contact are regulations (91.126, 91.127, 91.129); entry methods, pattern altitudes and CTAF calls are recommendations.

Propeller airplanes fly the pattern at 1,000 feet AGL and turbine airplanes at 1,500 feet AGL or higher, unless the Chart Supplement says otherwise. Stay at or below 200 knots near Class C and D airports.
Enter level at pattern altitude on the 45° at midfield. From the upwind side, cross 500 feet above pattern altitude, or 2,000 feet AGL where jets operate.
Hold altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots, and go around if you are not stabilized by 500 feet AGL (VMC) or the approach falls apart below 300 feet AGL.
Most midairs happen near the runway in good weather. Scan in 10° steps, uncover blind spots, keep lights on, and never rely on ADS-B or ATC alone.
Following a larger aircraft makes wake avoidance your job: stay at or above its path, land beyond its touchdown point, and wait 2 minutes after its touch-and-go.
At the first sign of a microburst, go around. Don't chase the first headwind gust with less power.
cfi_notes: Examiners like to ask which pattern items are regulatory. Drill the split: 91.126(b) turn direction, 91.126(d)/91.127(c) tower contact before 4 NM, 91.129 Class D items and 91.117 speeds are rules; the 45° entry, 1,000-foot TPA and CTAF calls come from AC 90-66C and the AIM.

Students often miss that a towered airport may sit in Class E or G airspace. 91.126(d) and 91.127(c) still require two-way radio with the tower before 4 NM, up to and including 2,500 feet AGL (AIM 4-3-2a explains why).

Source differences (the lesson follows the current AIM): AC 90-66C Appendix A and AFH 8-4 define the upwind leg as parallel to the runway in the landing direction; AIM 4-3-2c2 defines it as the straight-ahead extension of departure used by ATC. AC 90-66C 11.7 says turn crosswind within 300 feet below pattern altitude; the AIM key says within 300 feet of pattern altitude. Teach 'within 300 feet below.'

Commercial students flying complex airplanes lose altitude and speed control while configuring. Have them extend gear and flaps on a set schedule and retrim after every change; the ACS tolerance is still ±100 feet and ±10 knots.
Teach the stabilized approach gates from AFH 9-6 and make go-arounds normal. Fly at least one planned go-around per lesson so the student isn't tempted to save a bad approach on the checkride.
Instrument-rated students doing practice approaches at non-towered fields tend to give fix names on the CTAF. Make them give direction, distance and intentions (AC 90-66C 9.11.5).
Expect DPEs to probe wake responsibility after accepting 'follow the jet' or a visual approach (AIM 7-4-8b), and the meaning of an LLWAS alert versus a microburst alert (AIM 4-3-7).
gaps: Pattern speeds, power settings, flap and gear schedules are airplane-specific; use the POH/AFM. The sources give only generic guidance (1.4 VSO on base, 1.3 VSO on final, 70 to 90 knots on downwind for typical piston singles).

The sources give no step-by-step wind shear escape procedure for small single-engine airplanes. The AWH describes microburst effects and encounter studies but not a light-airplane technique; get it from the POH/AFM and your CFI.
Whether a part-time tower's airspace becomes Class E or Class G when the tower closes is published in the Chart Supplement for each airport, which is not among the uploaded sources.
Glider, parachute and ultralight pattern details (AC 90-66C Appendices B and C) and airport sign standards in detail (AC 150/5340-18H) are only touched on here.
The Task's elements for water landing areas are not taught here; this lesson covers single-engine land airplanes only.

activities.title: Must or should?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Left turns at a non-towered Class G airport unless markings show right turns
Talk to a Class E tower before 4 NM, up to 2,500 feet AGL
Get a clearance to land at an airport with an operating tower
Stay at or above the VASI glide path landing in Class D
Enter on a 45° to downwind abeam midfield
Fly a 1,000-foot AGL pattern in a piston airplane

activities.title: Key to the pattern
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Hold TPA until abeam approach end
Crosswind turn within 300 ft of TPA

activities.title: Where the information comes from
activities.intro: Tap a source, then what it gives you.

pairs.r: Tell ATC on first contact that you have it
Special conditions: check the Chart Supplement

activities.title: Pattern numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: A non-towered airport is 1,240 feet MSL and publishes no pattern altitude. You fly a piston single. What should the altimeter read on downwind?
items.why: Propeller airplanes fly the pattern at 1,000 feet AGL [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3a]]: 1,240 + 1,000 = 2,240 feet MSL.

items.q: You arrive from the upwind side of an airport at 680 feet MSL where business jets operate. At what MSL altitude do you cross midfield using the preferred entry?
items.why: With large or turbine aircraft at the airport, stay at 2,000 feet AGL [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]: 680 + 2,000 = 2,680 feet MSL.

items.q: Your POH approach speed is 80 KIAS. The AWOS reports wind 160 at 16 gusting 26. Using half the gust factor, what approach speed do you fly?
items.why: Gust factor = 26 - 16 = 10 knots. Half is 5: 80 + 5 = 85 KIAS [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Stay within the POH/AFM.

items.q: Following a jet on a visual approach with no glidepath guidance, you use the 3-to-1 principle. How high above touchdown should you be 4 miles out?
items.why: 3 to 1 means about 300 feet per mile: 3,000 feet at 10 miles, 1,500 at 5, 1,200 at 4 [[34:153|AIM 7-4-8e]]. 4 × 300 = 1,200 feet.

items.q: You fly at 150 knots and another airplane comes head-on at 130 knots. About how many NM close in the 12.5 seconds it takes to see, decide and start moving away?
items.why: Closing speed 150 + 130 = 280 knots. The reaction chain takes 12.5 seconds [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]]. 280 × 12.5 ÷ 3,600 = 0.97 NM.

activities.title: True or false: seeing and staying ahead
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: An airplane on a collision course grows steadily in the windshield, so you will see it coming early.
cards.why: False. Because of the blossom effect it seems motionless for a long time, then suddenly fills the window [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.8]].

cards.s: Scan in eye movements of no more than about 10°, looking at each area for at least 1 second.
cards.why: True. That is the effective scanning technique AC 90-48E recommends [[16:12|AC 90-48E 12]].

cards.s: From seeing traffic to the airplane starting to move away takes about 12.5 seconds.
cards.why: True. Recognition, decision, muscle reaction and aircraft lag add up to about 12.5 seconds [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]].

cards.s: With ADS-B In traffic on your display, you no longer need to scan as carefully.
cards.why: False. Traffic equipment does not relieve you of see-and-avoid, and displays can pull your eyes inside [[16:14|AC 90-48E 15]].

cards.s: At night, look straight at a dim light to see it best.
cards.why: False. The night blind spot is in the center of your vision; look about 10° off center [[16:13|AC 90-48E 13.1]].

cards.s: When overloaded in the pattern, stop, think, slow down and prioritize.
cards.why: True. That is the PHAK's fix for work overload [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

cards.s: Most midair collisions happen in poor visibility.
cards.why: False. Most happen in good visibility and daylight [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].

activities.title: Busy afternoon at Lakeview
activities.intro: You are flying N731CP, a retractable-gear single, to Lakeview, a non-towered airport in Class G airspace at 900 feet MSL. Runway 27 is in use with left traffic and a 1,000-foot AGL pattern. Business jets are based there. You are 14 miles north.

steps.s: The AWOS gives wind 260 at 12. The CTAF is busy. What next?
options: Call "any traffic in the area, please advise" to find out who is there
Self-announce your position, altitude and intentions about 10 miles out, and keep listening
Stay quiet until you enter downwind to keep the frequency clear
Ask UNICOM to sequence you into the pattern
steps.why: Arrivals should self-announce position, altitude and intentions about 10 miles out [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.1]]. "Traffic in the area, please advise" is not a recognized phrase [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g1]], and sequencing is not UNICOM's job [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.1]].

steps.s: You arrive from the north, the side opposite the left downwind for 27. A Cirrus is on downwind. How do you join?
options: Descend to 1,900 feet MSL and cut straight across midfield onto downwind
Cross midfield at 2,900 feet MSL, fly about 2 miles clear, descend to 1,900, then turn to a 45° entry
Fly a straight-in to Runway 27 to save time
Enter on a midfield crosswind at 1,900 feet even though the pattern is busy
steps.why: With jets based there, cross at 2,000 feet AGL (900 + 2,000 = 2,900 MSL), descend about 2 miles clear, and join on the 45°. The midfield crosswind entry should not be used when the pattern is busy [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

steps.s: Abeam midfield on downwind you hear: "Lakeview traffic, Citation on 4-mile final RNAV 27, full stop." The Cirrus is turning base. What do you do?
options: Turn base early to get in ahead of the jet
Announce you are extending downwind, and turn base only once you have the Citation in sight and can follow it
Make an unannounced 360 on downwind
Tell the Citation to go around because you are in the pattern
steps.why: An aircraft on final approach has the right-of-way over others in flight, and you may not cut in front of it [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]. Communicate your position and intentions [[17:12|AC 90-66C 10.1]].

steps.s: You follow the Citation onto final. Where do you plan to touch down?
options: Short of the Citation's touchdown point
Beyond its touchdown point, staying at or above its approach path
Exactly where it touched down
Anywhere: business jets leave no wake at landing speed
steps.why: Behind a larger aircraft on the same runway, stay at or above its final approach path, note its touchdown point, and land beyond it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b1]].

steps.s: At 350 feet AGL a gust leaves you 15 knots fast, high, and sinking 1,200 fpm. What now?
options: Push over and pull power to make the first third of the runway
Go around: you are not stabilized below 500 feet in VMC
Raise the flaps to stop the sink
Keep going and fix it in the flare
steps.why: Go around if not stabilized by 500 feet above the airport in VMC. 15 knots fast is outside the +10/-5 window, and 1,200 fpm is above the 500 to 1,000 fpm guide [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

steps.s: On the go-around, the Cirrus announces it is taking Runway 27 for departure. What is your best path?
options: Climb straight down the centerline, directly over the runway
Announce the go-around and, at a safe altitude, make a shallow turn to the upwind side so you can see the runway and the Cirrus
Turn left onto downwind right away at 400 feet
Descend to stay below the departing Cirrus
steps.why: At a safe altitude, make a shallow-bank turn to the upwind side for a better view of the runway and departing aircraft [[24:168|AFH 8-4]], and communicate your position [[17:12|AC 90-66C 10.1]].

final_quiz.q: An airport is 2,130 feet MSL and publishes no pattern altitude. You are flying a turboprop. What is the lowest recommended pattern altitude?
options: 3,130 feet MSL
3,630 feet MSL
4,130 feet MSL
1,500 feet MSL
final_quiz.why: Turbine-powered aircraft enter at not less than 1,500 feet AGL [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3a]]: 2,130 + 1,500 = 3,630 feet MSL. 1,500 MSL forgets the field elevation.

final_quiz.q: Your radio fails in VFR conditions just outside Class D airspace. What allows you to land at the primary airport?
options: Squawk 7600 and land; no clearance is needed
Circle until another airplane lands, then follow it
Land at once on the runway most nearly into the wind
Basic VFR weather, visual contact with the tower, and a clearance to land, such as a steady green light
final_quiz.why: Under VFR you may land if weather is at or above basic VFR minimums, you keep visual contact with the tower, and you receive a clearance to land [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)(2)]]. Steady green to an aircraft in flight means cleared to land [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

final_quiz.q: Your DPE wants to practice several landings and asks you to request "the option." Where can you use it?
options: Only at airports with an operational control tower, subject to ATC approval
At any airport, by announcing it on the CTAF
Only at non-towered airports, to avoid tower workload
Only on an IFR flight plan
final_quiz.why: The option procedure is used only where there is an operational control tower and is subject to ATC approval. Request it entering downwind for a VFR pattern [[33:265|AIM 4-3-23]] [[33:266|AIM 4-3-23]].

final_quiz.q: You fly a practice RNAV approach to a non-towered airport in VMC. Which set of CTAF calls follows the AIM?
options: Only when crossing the runway threshold
Only when starting the missed approach
Departing the FAF inbound, established on final, on completion or termination, and on the missed approach
Once at the initial approach fix, then only if asked
final_quiz.why: Announce departing the FAF inbound, established on the final segment, on completion or termination, and on executing the missed approach [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g6]].

final_quiz.q: At a towered airport you are catching up to the airplane ahead on downwind. Which is acceptable without first asking the controller?
options: A 360 to open the gap
Shallow S-turns or slowing down
Turning base early to get ahead of it
Climbing 500 feet above pattern altitude
final_quiz.why: Controllers can anticipate minor maneuvering such as shallow S-turns, but not a 360. A 360 in the pattern should never be made without first advising the controller [[33:244|AIM 4-3-5]] [[33:245|AIM 4-3-5]].

final_quiz.q: You accept a visual approach behind a Boeing 737. No glidepath guidance is available. What is the best wake plan?
options: Stay below its path and touch down short of its touchdown point
Ask the tower to provide wake separation, since that is ATC's job
Fly the same path and land at the same point
Fly on or above a 3-to-1 glidepath and land beyond its touchdown point
final_quiz.why: Accepting a visual approach accepts wake separation responsibility [[34:153|AIM 7-4-8b]]. Fly on or above the glidepath, using 3-to-1 without guidance, and land beyond the heavier aircraft's touchdown point [[34:153|AIM 7-4-8e]] [[34:154|AIM 7-4-8e]].

final_quiz.q: On final, the PAPI shows three white lights and one red. What does it mean?
options: Slightly high, about 3.2°
On glide path
Slightly low, about 2.8°
High, more than 3.5°
final_quiz.why: Three white and one red is slightly high, about 3.2°. Two and two is on path; all white is high [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2b]].

final_quiz.q: In a normal VFR pattern, a sudden gust upsets your approach at 250 feet AGL. What does the AFH recommend?
options: Fix it, since the 500-foot gate is already past
Add flaps and continue
Go around immediately: unstabilized below 300 feet AGL
Slow below the landing speed to steepen the descent
final_quiz.why: For a typical GA piston aircraft in a pattern, an immediate go-around should be started if the approach becomes unstabilized below 300 feet AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

final_quiz.q: On a 5-mile final for Runway 17, you hear: "Runway 17 arrival microburst alert, 40 knot loss 3 mile final." What is the best choice?
options: Continue; you will be through it in under a minute
Add 20 knots and continue
Descend below the microburst and continue
Break off the approach and hold clear or divert; microbursts seldom last more than 15 minutes
final_quiz.why: A 40-knot loss on short final can be beyond recovery at low altitude [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]. An individual microburst seldom lasts more than 15 minutes after reaching the ground, so wait it out or divert [[34:108|AIM 7-1-24d]].

final_quiz.q: You fly at 160 knots and another airplane approaches head-on at 140 knots. About how far apart are you when you must spot it, if avoidance takes 12.5 seconds to begin?
options: About 0.25 NM
About 0.5 NM
About 1 NM
About 2 NM
final_quiz.why: Closing speed 160 + 140 = 300 knots. It takes about 12.5 seconds before the airplane begins to move [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]]. 300 × 12.5 ÷ 3,600 = 1.04 NM, so about 1 NM just to start the turn.

final_quiz.q: A non-towered airport is 1,100 feet MSL with a 1,000-foot AGL pattern and no jet traffic. You arrive from the upwind side. At what altitude should you cross midfield?
options: 2,600 feet MSL
2,100 feet MSL
3,100 feet MSL
1,600 feet MSL
final_quiz.why: Cross at least 500 feet above pattern altitude, normally 1,500 feet AGL [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]: 1,100 + 1,500 = 2,600 feet MSL.

final_quiz.q: On downwind at a non-towered airport, an ultralight converges from your right at your altitude. Who must give way?
options: You, because it is on your right
The ultralight; ultralights must yield to all aircraft
Whoever is lower
Neither; ultralights don't use the pattern
final_quiz.why: Ultralight vehicles are required to yield the right-of-way to all aircraft [[17:17|AC 90-66C 12.3.1]]. Still see and avoid, since you may not pass over, under or ahead unless well clear [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].

final_quiz.q: An airport has an operating tower but no weather reporting, so it has no Class D airspace. What must you do?
options: Nothing; without Class D no contact is required
Contact the tower only when on final
Self-announce on the CTAF instead of the tower
Make two-way radio contact with the tower before 4 NM, up to and including 2,500 feet AGL
final_quiz.why: At an airport with an operational tower in Class E or G airspace, communications must be established before 4 NM, up to and including 2,500 feet AGL [[60:452|14 CFR 91.126(d)]] [[60:452|14 CFR 91.127(c)]]. AIM 4-3-2a describes these towered airports without Class D [[33:237|AIM 4-3-2a]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH approach speed is 76 KIAS. The ATIS gives wind 200 at 20 gusting 32. What final approach speed fits the common rule?
options: 76 KIAS
82 KIAS
88 KIAS
108 KIAS
final_quiz.why: Gust factor = 32 - 20 = 12 knots; half is 6. 76 + 6 = 82 KIAS [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Adding the whole gust (88) or the whole wind is too fast.
